questions.q: A hollow, right circular cone of base radius $R$ and height $h$, with its tip at the origin is rotating about the $Z$-axis with an angular velocity $\omega$, as shown in the figure. The cone carries a total charge $Q$ uniformly distributed on its curved surface. The magnitude of magnetic field at a point $(0, 0, z)$, where $z \gg R$ and $z \gg h$, is $\dfrac{n\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{Q R^2 \omega}{z^3}$. The value of $n$ is:
questions.solution:
For a point on the axis at a distance $z \gg R$ and $z \gg h$, the rotating cone can be considered as a magnetic dipole. The magnetic field on the axis of a dipole is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{2M}{z^3}$

where $M$ is the magnetic dipole moment of the cone.

To find $M$, consider an elemental ring on the cone at a vertical distance $y$ from the origin, with vertical thickness $dy$. The radius of this ring is $r = \dfrac{R}{h}y$ and its slant length is $dl = \dfrac{\sqrt{R^2+h^2}}{h}dy$.

The surface charge density of the cone is $\sigma = \dfrac{Q}{\pi R \sqrt{R^2+h^2}}$.

The charge on the elemental ring is:

$dq = \sigma (2\pi r dl) = \dfrac{Q}{\pi R \sqrt{R^2+h^2}} \left(2\pi \dfrac{R}{h}y \dfrac{\sqrt{R^2+h^2}}{h}dy\right) = \dfrac{2Q}{h^2}y dy$

The current due to the rotation of this ring is:

$dI = \dfrac{dq}{T} = \dfrac{dq \omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{Q\omega}{\pi h^2}y dy$

The magnetic moment of this elemental ring is:

$dM = dI (\pi r^2) = \left(\dfrac{Q\omega}{\pi h^2}y dy\right) \pi \left(\dfrac{R}{h}y\right)^2 = \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{h^4}y^3 dy$

Integrating from $y = 0$ to $y = h$, the total magnetic moment is:

$M = \int_{0}^{h} \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{h^4}y^3 dy = \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{h^4} \left[\dfrac{y^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{h} = \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{4}$

Alternatively, using the gyromagnetic ratio for a uniform charge distribution, $\dfrac{M}{L_{ang}} = \dfrac{Q}{2m}$. The moment of inertia of a hollow cone is $I = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2$, so the angular momentum is $L_{ang} = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\omega$. Thus, $M = \dfrac{Q}{2m} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\omega\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}QR^2\omega$.

Substituting $M$ into the magnetic field formula:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{2}{z^3} \left(\dfrac{1}{4}QR^2\omega\right) = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{QR^2\omega}{2z^3}$

Comparing this with the given expression $B = \dfrac{n\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{QR^2\omega}{z^3}$, we get:

$n = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$

Answer: $0.5$

questions.q: In a vacuum chamber, a particle of charge $1\ \mu\text{C}$ and mass $1$ mg is projected with a velocity $(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$ ms$^{-1}$ from the $XZ$ plane at time $t = 0$ in an electric field of $1\hat{i}$ Vm$^{-1}$. At $t = 0.2$ s, the electric field is switched off and a magnetic field of $6\hat{j}$ T is switched on. The acceleration due to gravity is $-10\hat{j}$ ms$^{-2}$. Correct option(s) is/are:
options: The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.3$ s is $15$ cm.
The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.4$ s is $10$ cm.
The radius of the trajectory of the particle for $t > 0.2$ s is $20$ cm.
The particle will be in the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.35$ s.
questions.solution:
For the time interval $0 \le t \le 0.2$ s, the particle is under the influence of the electric field and gravity.
The charge-to-mass ratio of the particle is $\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{10^{-6}} = 1$ C kg$^{-1}$.

The acceleration of the particle is:
$\vec{a} = \dfrac{q\vec{E}}{m} + \vec{g} = 1(\hat{i}) - 10\hat{j} = \hat{i} - 10\hat{j}$ ms$^{-2}$

Given the initial velocity $\vec{v}_0 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$ ms$^{-1}$ and initial vertical position $y_0 = 0$ (since it is projected from the $XZ$ plane), we can find the velocity and position at $t = 0.2$ s.

Velocity at $t = 0.2$ s:
$\vec{v}(0.2) = \vec{v}_0 + \vec{a}t = (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) + (\hat{i} - 10\hat{j})(0.2) = 1.2\hat{i}$ ms$^{-1}$

Vertical position at $t = 0.2$ s:
$y(0.2) = y_0 + v_{0y}t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_y t^2 = 0 + 2(0.2) - \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(0.2)^2 = 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.2$ m $= 20$ cm

For $t > 0.2$ s, the electric field is switched off and the magnetic field $\vec{B} = 6\hat{j}$ T is switched on. The magnetic force $\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ acts only in the $XZ$ plane because $\vec{B}$ is along the $y$-axis. The vertical motion is only affected by gravity.

Let $t' = t - 0.2$ be the time elapsed after the fields are switched. The initial vertical velocity for this phase is $v_y(0.2) = 0$.
The vertical position as a function of $t'$ is:
$y(t') = y(0.2) + v_y(0.2)t' - \dfrac{1}{2}gt'^2 = 0.2 - 5t'^2$

Evaluating the options:
At $t = 0.3$ s ($t' = 0.1$ s):
$y(0.1) = 0.2 - 5(0.1)^2 = 0.2 - 0.05 = 0.15$ m $= 15$ cm. (Option A is correct)

At $t = 0.4$ s ($t' = 0.2$ s):
$y(0.2) = 0.2 - 5(0.2)^2 = 0.2 - 0.2 = 0$ m $= 0$ cm. (Option B is incorrect)

At $t = 0.35$ s ($t' = 0.15$ s):
$y(0.15) = 0.2 - 5(0.15)^2 = 0.2 - 0.1125 = 0.0875$ m $\neq 0$. (Option D is incorrect)

For the radius of the trajectory for $t > 0.2$ s, the particle moves in a helical path. The radius of the circular projection in the $XZ$ plane is determined by the velocity perpendicular to the magnetic field, $v_{\perp} = 1.2$ ms$^{-1}$.
$R = \dfrac{mv_{\perp}}{qB} = \dfrac{10^{-6} \times 1.2}{10^{-6} \times 6} = 0.2$ m $= 20$ cm. (Option C is correct)

Answer: The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.3$ s is $15$ cm.; The radius of the trajectory of the particle for $t > 0.2$ s is $20$ cm.

The ratio of the magnitudes of the magnetic dipole moment to the angular momentum about the same axis is given as $\alpha \frac{Q}{2 M}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______ .

An infinitely long wire, located on the $z$-axis, carries a current $I$ along the $+z$-direction and produces the magnetic field $\vec{B}$. The magnitude of the line integral $\int \vec{B} \cdot \overrightarrow{d l}$ along a straight line from the point $(-\sqrt{3} a, a, 0)$ to $(a, a, 0)$ is given by
[ $\mu_0$ is the magnetic permeability of free space.]
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \ell}|=\mathrm{rd} \theta \\ & \Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \\ & \Rightarrow \int \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \ell}=\int|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}||\overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \ell}| \cos 0^{\circ} \\ & =\int\left(\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}}\right) \times(\operatorname{rd} \theta) \\ & =\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi} \mathrm{d} \theta=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi}\left[\theta_2-\left(-\theta_1\right)\right]\end{aligned}$
[ $\theta_1$ is anticlockwise hence taken negative]

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \tan \theta_1=\frac{\mathrm{a} \sqrt{3}}{\mathrm{a}}=\sqrt{3} \\ & \theta_1=\frac{\pi}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \tan \theta_2=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{a}}=1 \\ & \theta_2=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ & \Rightarrow \int \mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \ell=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi}\left[\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right] \\ & =\frac{7 \mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{24} \\ & \Rightarrow \text{ Ans. Option (1) }\end{aligned}$

A small circular loop of area $A$ and resistance $R$ is fixed on a horizontal $xy$-plane with the center of the loop always on the axis $\overset{^}{n}$ of a long solenoid. The solenoid has $m$ turns per unit length and carries current $I$ counter clockwise as shown in the figure. The magnetic field due to the solenoid is in $\overset{^}{n}$ direction. List-I gives time dependences of $\overset{^}{n}$ in terms of a constant angular frequency $\omega$. List-II gives the torques experienced by the circular loop at time $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6\omega}$, Let $\alpha = \dfrac{{A}^{2}{\mu}_{0}^{2}{m}^{2}{I}^{2}\omega}{2R}$.

List-I List-II
(i) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{j} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)$ (p) $0$
(ii) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{i} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{j}\right)$ (q) $- \dfrac{\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$
(iii) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{i} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)$ (r) $\dfrac{3\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$
(iv) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(cos\omegat\overset{^}{j} + sin\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)$ (s) $\dfrac{\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{j}$
(t) $- \dfrac{3\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: $i \to q, ii \to p, iii \to s, iv \to t$
$i \to s, ii \to t, iii \to q, iv \to p$
$i \to q, ii \to p, iii \to s, iv \to r$
$i \to t, ii \to q, iii \to p, iv \to r$
questions.solution:
Note: This question was given bonus by JEE council.

The magnetic field in a solenoid is given by, $\overset{\to}{B} = {\mu}_{0}mI\overset{^}{n}$. Therefore, the flux through the loop will be,

$ϕ = \left(A\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left({\mu}_{0}mI\overset{^}{n}\right)$

For case I:

$ϕ = \dfrac{BA}{\sqrt{2}}cos\left(\omegat\right)$

The emf will be,

$ε = \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

Therefore, the current in the loop will be,

$i = \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

The magnetic moment of the loop will be,

$\overset{\to}{m} = iA\overset{^}{k} = \dfrac{B{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{k}$

Therefore, the torque

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{m} \times \overset{\to}{B} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\left(\overset{^}{k} \times \overset{^}{n}\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{τ} = - \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left[\overset{^}{i}\right]\sin^{2}\left(\omegat\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{τ} = - \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left[\sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right] = \dfrac{- \alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$

Hence, $\left(I\right) \to q$

For case II

$ϕ = 0$

Therefore, we can directly write $τ = 0$

Hence $\left(II\right) \to p$

Following the same process as in case I for case III

$ϕ = \dfrac{BA}{\sqrt{2}}cos\left(\omegat\right)$

$i = \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

$\overset{\to}{m} = \dfrac{B{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{m} \times \overset{\to}{B} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}R}sin\omegat\left(\overset{^}{k} \times \left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{i} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omegasin\left(\omegat\right)}{2R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\sin^{2}\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \dfrac{\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{j}$

Hence, $III \to s$

Following the same process as in case I for case IV

$ϕ = \dfrac{BA}{\sqrt{2}}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

$i = - \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}cos\left(\omegat\right)$

$\overset{\to}{m} = - \dfrac{B{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}cos\omegat\left(\overset{^}{k}\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{m} \times \overset{\to}{B} = - \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left(\overset{^}{k} \times \overset{^}{j}\right)\cos^{2}\left(\omegat\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = + \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left(\overset{^}{i}\right) \cdot \cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = + \dfrac{3}{4}\alpha\overset{^}{i}$

Hence, $\left(IV\right) \to r$

Paragraph
A special metal $S$ conducts electricity without any resistance. A closed wire loop, made of $S$, does not allow any change in flux through itself by inducing a suitable current to generate a compensating flux. The induced current in the loop cannot decay due to its zero resistance. This current gives rise to a magnetic moment which in turn repels the source of magnetic field or flux. Consider such a loop, of radius $a$, with its center at the origin. A magnetic dipole of moment $m$ is brought along the axis of this loop from infinity to a point at distance $r(\gg a)$ from the center of the loop with its north pole always facing the loop, as shown in the figure below.

The magnitude of magnetic field of a dipole $m$, at a point on its axis at distance $r$, is $\frac{\mu_{0}}{2 \pi} \frac{m}{r^{3}}$, where $\mu_{0}$ is the permeability of free space. The magnitude of the force between two magnetic dipoles with moments, $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$, separated by a distance $r$ on the common axis, with their north poles facing each other, is $\frac{k m_{1} m_{2}}{r^{4}}$, where $k$ is a constant of appropriate dimensions. The direction of this force is along the line joining the two dipoles.

QuestionThe work done in bringing the dipole from infinity to a distance $r$ from the centre of the loop by the given process is proportional to:
questions.solution:
For a super conducting loop, net flux passing through it will remain constant.

${\left({ϕ}_{total}\right)}_{i} = {\left({ϕ}_{total}\right)}_{f}$

As area is same, therefore,

$\dfrac{{\mu}_{0}m}{2{\pi r}^{3}} = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2a}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{am}{{\pi r}^{3}}$

$⇒ I ∝ \dfrac{m}{{r}^{3}}$

The current carrying superconducting loop will also behave like a magnet, whose magnetic dipole moment is given by,${m}_{1} = NIA = ( 1 ) \left(\dfrac{am}{{\pi r}^{3}}\right) \times \pi{a}^{2} = \dfrac{m{a}^{3}}{{r}^{3}}$

$⇒ {m}_{1} ∝ \dfrac{m}{{r}^{3}}$

The repulsive force felt on the magnet will be

$F = \dfrac{K{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{4}} = \dfrac{\left({K}^{'}\right)\left(\dfrac{m}{{r}^{3}}\right)\left(m\right)}{{r}^{4}} ∝ \dfrac{{m}^{2}}{{r}^{7}}$

${W}_{ext} = - ∫ Fdr = - K ' ∫ \dfrac{{m}^{2}}{{r}^{7}}dr$

Using $∫ {x}^{n}dx = \dfrac{{x}^{n + 1}}{n + 1}$

We get,

${W}_{ext} ∝ \dfrac{{m}^{2}}{{r}^{6}}$

questions.q: An $\alpha$-particle (mass $4$ amu) and a singly charged Sulphur ion (mass $32$ amu) are initially at rest. They are accelerated through a potential $V$ and then allowed to pass into a region of uniform magnetic field which is normal to the velocities of the particles. Within this region, the $\alpha$-particle and the sulphur ion move in circular orbits of radii ${R}_{\alpha} and {R}_{S}$, respectively. The ratio $\left(\dfrac{{R}_{S}}{{R}_{\alpha}}\right)$ is __________ .
questions.solution:
When a particle moves on a circular path in a magnetic field then,

$∵ R = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mE}}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mV}}{\sqrt{q}B}$

According to given data,

$∵ V = \text{constant}\text{\text{ and }}B = \text{constant}$

$∴ R ∝ \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{q}}$

$\dfrac{{R}_{\alpha}}{{R}_{S}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{m}_{\alpha}}{{q}_{\alpha}} \times \dfrac{{q}_{S}}{{m}_{S}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{32}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{R}_{\alpha}}{{R}_{S}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Then, $\dfrac{{R}_{S}}{{R}_{\alpha}} = 4$

One of them is converted into a voltmeter of $100mV$ full scale reading and the other into an Ammeter of $1mA$ full scale current using appropriate resistors. The measured value of  $R$  will be  $978Ω < R < 982Ω .$

If the ideal cell is replaced by a cell having internal resistance of  $5Ω$  then the measured value of  $R$  will be more than  $1000Ω .$

Voltmeter rom galvanometer arrangement.
Given: ${R}_{g} = 10Ω$ and ${I}_{g} = 2\muA$
Required voltage range, $V = 100 \times {10}^{- 3}volts$
$⇒ V = {I}_{g}\left({R}_{g} + {R}_{v}\right) = {10}^{- 1}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{10}^{- 1}}{2 \times {10}^{- 6}} = {R}_{g} + {R}_{v}\left(as, {I}_{g} = 2\muA\right)$
$⇒ 5 \times {10}^{4}Ω \approx {R}_{v} ( {R}_{v} < {10}^{5}Ω ) ⇒$ Option $( A )$ is incorrect.

Galvanometer to Ammeter arrangement
$\Delta{V}_{G} = \Delta{V}_{S}$
${I}_{g} ⋅ {R}_{g} = \left(I - {I}_{g}\right) ⋅ S$
$⇒ S = \dfrac{{I}_{g} ⋅ {R}_{g}}{I - {I}_{g}} = \dfrac{2 \times {10}^{- 6} \times 10}{{10}^{- 3} - 2 \times {10}^{- 6}}$
$⇒ S = 2 \times {10}^{- 5} \times {10}^{3} = 2 \times {10}^{- 2}$
$⇒ S = 20mΩ ⇒ ( C )$ is correct.
Circuit diagram for ohm's law

Resistance ammeter,
${R}_{A} = \dfrac{20 \times {10}^{- 3} \times 10}{10} = 20 \times {10}^{- 3}Ω$
$i = \dfrac{ε}{\left(\dfrac{1000 \times 50 \times {10}^{3}}{51 \times {10}^{3}}\right)} = \dfrac{51ε}{5 \times {10}^{4}}\left(∵ {R}_{A} \to 0\right)$
${i}^{′} = i\left(\dfrac{{R}_{v}}{51 \times {10}^{3}}\right) = \dfrac{ε}{1000}$
Measured resistance $∴ {R}_{m} = \dfrac{{i}^{′} \times 1000}{i} = \dfrac{ε}{51ε} \times 5 \times {10}^{4} = \dfrac{5 \times {10}^{4}}{51} = 980.4Ω$
If the voltmeter shows full scale deflection then
$\dfrac{ε}{980} \times \left(\dfrac{1000}{51 \times {10}^{3}}\right) \times 5 \times {10}^{4} = {10}^{- 1}$
$∴ ε = 999.6mv$

&\text{ since } \mathrm{B}_1=\frac{\mathrm{B}_2}{4}
\end{aligned}\)

Time$ in $\(B_1 \Rightarrow \frac{\pi B}{q B_1}=t_1\)

Total distance along \(\mathrm{x}\)-axis \(\mathrm{d}_1+\mathrm{d}_2=2 \mathrm{r}_1+2 \mathrm{r}_2=2\left(\mathrm{r}_1+\mathrm{r}_2\right)=2\left(5 \mathrm{r}_2\right)\)

questions.q: A steady current $I$ flows along an infinitely long hollow cylindrical conductor of radius $R$. This cylinder is placed co-axially inside an infinite solenoid of radius $2R$. The solenoid has $n$ turns per unit length and carries a steady current $I$. Consider a point $P$ at a distance $r$ from the common axis. The correct statement(s) is(are):
options: In the region $0 < r < R$, the magnetic field is non-zero.
In the region $R < r < 2R$, the magnetic field is along the common axis.
In the region $R < r < 2R$, the magnetic field is tangential to the circle of radius $r$, centered on the axis.
In the region $r > 2R,$ the magnetic field is non-zero.
questions.solution:
If we consider a point at a distance $r$ from a common axis such that $0 < r < R$, the magnetic field is non-zero because inside infinite solenoid magnetic field is, $\overset{\to}{B} = {\mu}_{0}ni$ and due to the hollow cylinder it is zero. Hence, net magnetic field is non-zero.

If $2R < r$, then magnetic field due to an infinite solenoid is zero but there will be a non-zero magnetic field because of hollow cylinder. Hence, net magnetic field is non-zero.

If $R < r < 2R$, then the magnetic field due to solenoid is along the axis and magnetic field due to the hollow cylinder is in circular form. Hence, the net magnetic field is neither along axis nor in tangential direction.
